newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia faces doctors' decision on Yeltsin surgery.
newsitem.headline: Russia faces doctors' decision on Yeltsin surgery.

text.p: Russia faces a critical test on Wednesday when doctors decide whether President Boris Yeltsin is well enough to undergo heart bypass surgery.

If they say no, the man who holds supreme power in the world's largest country will be under doctors' orders to rest, fuelling a drive by his communist opponents to force him from the Kremlin just three months into his second term.
If they say yes, Yeltsin risks complications which doctors have said could range from pneumonia to kidney failure.
The 65-year-old president, used to giving the orders, will meet with a team of doctors in the hospital where he has been receiving treatment at about noon (0900 GMT) on Wednesday to hear his fate.
The surgeon chosen to lead the operation has hinted that the doctors may decide to put the operation off for up to eight weeks, hoping the president will be well enough by then.

On Tuesday Yeltsin had trouble speaking in a brief and heavily-edited television clip released by the Kremlin, an appearance which the communists are sure to seize upon in their campaign for him to step down.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin said on Tuesday Yeltsin's resignation now was out of the question and condemned the opposition call. "This is totally unacceptable and should not even be mentioned at the moment," he said.
Yeltsin has already handed over some powers to Chernomyrdin and said he would put the prime minister in complete charge while he is in the operating theatre.

Under the constitution, Chernomyrdin steps in if Yeltsin becomes incapacitated but there is no mechanism for this. Some analysts say officials will do everything they can to stop the handover, which would require an election within three months.

But the president's absence from the political scene -- he has been in hospital for 10 days and out of the public eye since early July -- has left Chernomyrdin, security chief Lebed and Moscow mayor Yuri Luzhkov jostling for power.

Lebed, who has made no secret of his presidential ambitions, caused a stir on Tuesday when he was quoted as threatening western industrial interests in Russia if NATO went ahead with its plans to take in its former communist allies.

The government denied it had any such intentions and a spokesman for Lebed -- who has been in trouble before with controversial off-the-cuff remarks -- said the general had made no such statement. The newspaper stuck by its story.

Yeltsin dropped the bombshell of his forthcoming heart operation in a television interview on September 5. He said confidently that it would take place at the end of the month and that doctors had told him it would be straightforward.
Since then, despite calming statements from the Kremlin, it has become apparent that the state of his health is causing concern among those who will take the decision to operate.

Cardiac surgeon Renat Akchurin disclosed that the condition of Yeltsin's heart indicated he had had a heart attack -- his third -- around the time he suddenly dropped out of sight just before the second round of the presidential election in July.
In comments at the weekend, Akchurin also said it may be too dangerous to operate, but on Tuesday ruled out the possibility that the surgery could be scrapped.

Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzembsky said the doctors would discuss the "date, tactics and the extent of the forthcoming operation", raising the possibilty that doctors might decide on a less interventionary technique than open heart surgery.
